doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Hampton pay dispute and a first business lesson
summary: Promised $75 a night, he was paid on $60; he learned to get things in writing and talks about handshake agreements.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: But can I ask you, what the gig ended up paying, with Hampton, at that point? Because he didn’t have a reputation for —

Well see time has gone by so I’ll publicly tell the whole thing to you. But I’ll try to leave as many names out as possible. I was told by someone that Europe was another story. The payment in Europe was good so I’ll leave that alone. Very fair, very good. So by summer when we get back to the States, you will make $75 a night when we work. I said yeah it sounds great. I mean look when you’re in college, and somebody says you’re going to make $50 you scream and hollar. So I said great, beautiful. So we got to the States and I wanted a single room, because you want to practice and do my stuff. Most of the guys were doubles, I said I’m going to get a single room. Well my room was $60 for the night. Okay. I got my first paycheck and it was based upon $60 a night. So I told this person I said, “Excuse me, when we discussed this, it was $75.” “What are you trying to rip me off? I said $60.” So I learned the flip flop that people do. It was my first business lesson, right out of college, how people — maybe try to get things in writing. And you know my father always said always read what you sign, and always try to get what — And to this day, one thing I notice these days, this has nothing to do with music. I went to rent a car the other day and they wanted to have me sign something. People get nervous if you read what they want you to sign. They’ll look: what are you reading! I’m reading what you © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

told me to sign. Well it just says that you’re going to rent the car and if you do any damage — Well let me read that then! And then I said, “Well this here says that you’re going to charge my card, that this document charges my card if it gets damaged, but there’s no damages yet. I can sign this after. They say, “No, no, we just do that —” I say, “No that’s not what this says. It says I agree to pay for the damages on the car. There’s no damages on the car so you can’t charge my credit card. I said you could just mark this sheet and say that there are damages if I sign it at the bottom. Well uh, so then I don’t sign it see? So people, they even get — so that was my first business lesson was with Lionel Hampton, to try to see if you can get things in writing. Some people are reluctant too and sometimes there are certain people you do have to trust. There’s a lot of guys to this day, a lot of the older jazz musicians, they don’t do contracts, they don’t — but they are people of their word. I know guys say they know promoters in Europe — I just don’t want to name any names, but — but they have great relationships with them, word of mouth. And that’s very important too, your bond and your word. Look, they have a friend in Europe who says, “Look, I’ll book a tour for you, it’ll be three weeks, pay you this much, I’ll send you a ticket in a couple of weeks.” They both agree to it and that’s it, and everything’s straight. And I have those agreements myself with people in Europe and all, nothing written down. And then I have people that especially have to have things written down. So my first good business lesson was with Lionel.
